title: Scammers Exploit 2026 U.S. Midterm Election to Perpetrate Multiple Fraud Schemes

result.summary: Election-Related Fraud Schemes Exploiting 2026 Midterm Election

claims.text: The FBI issued a public service announcement on 15 October 2026 warning that scammers are exploiting the 2026 U.S. Midterm Election to perpetrate financial fraud schemes targeting U.S. residents. These schemes include fraudulent campaign donation solicitations, non-delivery of political merchandise, and phishing for personally identifiable information (PII) via fake voter registration pages. Scammers use AI-generated voices, images, and messages to impersonate candidates, campaigns, and government entities, increasing the realism and detectability challenges of these frauds. The FBI notes these tactics have been used in prior elections, including the 2024 U.S. General Election, and urges the public to verify organizations through the Federal Election Commission (FEC) website and report incidents to the Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3).

evidence.quote: The FBI warns the public that scammers could exploit the 2026 US Midterm Election to perpetrate financial fraud schemes.

As previously reported, scammers use the names, images, logos, and slogans of candidates to fraudulently solicit campaign contributions, sell merchandise that is never delivered, or steal personally identifiable information (PII) that can be used for other fraud.

Scammers also exploit artificial intelligence (AI) tools to generate highly realistic voices, images, and written messages that impersonate candidates, campaigns, government entities, and trusted contacts.
The realism makes these schemes harder for victims to detect and increases the likelihood of financial loss or exposure of PII.
Election-related fraud schemes come in many varieties, including the schemes detailed below.
Political Action Committee Scheme (a.k.a.

Scammers dupe victims into believing they are donating to a legitimate Political Action Committee (PAC), such as a Super PAC or candidate's campaign committee but the scammers have no affiliation with the PAC and keep the funds.
Scammers claim to sell political merchandise but do not ship the purchase when ordered.
This is a classic "non-shipment scam" or "non-delivery fraud" scheme.
Victims receive a text message or email stating they are not registered to vote in their state and are encouraged to click a link that takes the victim to a fraudulent state voter registration page.
This scheme is a means to steal PII for identity theft and potentially to further target victims for additional fraud schemes.
Verify and review the Political Action, Party, or Candidate Committee registration and financial filings on the Federal Election Commission (FEC) website.
Be mindful some scam PACs and SuperPACs may appear registered; if a PAC or SuperPAC reports high expenses for fundraising, consulting, compliance, or other administrative costs it may be a scam.
Confirm unsolicited contact information is associated with the organization it claims to represent.
Research companies before making purchases by checking reviews and complaints on BBB.org.
Check your voter registration at www.vote.gov.
If you or someone you know encounters an election-related scam, report it to your local FBI field office or to the Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) at www.ic3.gov.
Provide as much detail as possible:
The name of the person or company that contacted you.
Identifying information about the company and/or individuals who contacted you, including phone number, address, email address, and websites.
Financial transaction information including method of payment.

Describe your interaction with the individual, including how contact was initiated, the type of communication, what you were told or instructed, what you provided, and any other details pertinent to your complaint.
For additional information on other election-related threats, please see the following Public Service Announcements:

implications.text: Fraud schemes exploiting election cycles may increase the volume and sophistication of impersonation attacks targeting individuals and organizations, potentially leading to higher rates of financial loss and PII compromise. The use of AI to generate realistic impersonations raises the risk of successful social engineering, particularly in high-stakes periods like elections, where public attention and urgency are heightened.

evidence.quote: Scammers also exploit artificial intelligence (AI) tools to generate highly realistic voices, images, and written messages that impersonate candidates, campaigns, government entities, and trusted contacts.
The realism makes these schemes harder for victims to detect and increases the likelihood of financial loss or exposure of PII.

executive_summary.text: The FBI issued a public service announcement warning of fraud schemes exploiting the 2026 U.S. Midterm Election. Scammers use candidate names, logos, and AI-generated content to solicit fake campaign donations, sell non-delivered merchandise, steal personally identifiable information (PII), and impersonate government entities. These schemes target U.S. residents through unsolicited communications and have been observed in prior elections. The FBI urges the public to verify organizations via the FEC website and report incidents to IC3.

claims.text: The Federal Reserve reported that in August 2026, total consumer credit increased at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.9 percent, with revolving credit decreasing at an annual rate of 4.2 percent and nonrevolving credit increasing at 4.1 percent. The data include most credit extended to individuals, excluding loans secured by real estate, and are based on reporting from depository institutions, finance companies, credit unions, and federal government entities.

evidence.quote: (Eastern Time) August 2026 October 7, 2026 In August, consumer credit increased at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.9 percent.
Revolving credit decreased at an annual rate of 4.2 percent, while nonrevolving credit increased at an annual rate of 4.1 percent.
Covers most credit extended to individuals, excluding loans secured by real estate.

Includes receivables carried on the balance sheet of the institution as well as outstanding balances of pools upon which securities have been issued; under the current accounting rule, most of those balances remain on the balance sheets of the loan originator.

implications.text: A sustained decline in revolving credit, such as credit card balances, may indicate tighter consumer borrowing conditions or reduced consumer spending, which could affect credit quality and default risk in the near term.
